articles.title: Vigilance unearths irregularities in sports councils in Keralam
articles.description: VACB's Operation Kalikkalam exposes widespread financial irregularities and corruption in Kerala state and district sports councils, including fund diversion, non-tender procurements, and undistributed equipment.

articles.title: What’s on the menu for Xi at Trump’s state dinner
articles.description: Washington: President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will host Chinese President Xi Jinping and Madame Peng Liyuan at a White House state dinner on Thursday evening (Friday morning India time), with a menu that pairs American ingredients with Chinese influences. The dinner will be held in the East Room. The official delegations will join business leaders and government officials, according to details released by the Office of the First Lady. Melania Trump led preparations for the event. The meal will open with a toast of Schramsberg “Blanc De Noir”, an American sparkling wine chosen to recall a toast shared by President Richard Nixon and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing in 1972. Dinner begins with a yellow squash velouté served with a wild mushroom fricassée, crispy pancetta, and scallion oil. The release describes the soup as a smooth preparation of sweet yellow squash, with mushrooms sautéed in fresh herbs. The pancetta will add a savoury, smoky note, while the scallion oil will finish the dish. The main course will be sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a green herb sauce. The toasted sesame coating is intended to give the fish a nutty crust while keeping it tender. The vegetables will bring a mix of crisp and roasted textures to the plate. For dessert, guests will be served vanilla crémeux and White House honey ice cream with walnut frangipane and sour cherry confit. The dessert is fruit-shaped, with the cherry confit at its centre. Its ice cream will be made with honey harvested at the White House. The three courses bring together ingredients associated with American cooking and touches drawn from Chinese cuisine. Scallion oil finishes the opening dish; sesame and bok choy feature in the fish course. The White House described the menu as an effort to bring the culinary traditions of both countries together. Classically trained tenor Christopher Macchio will headline the entertainment. He performed at Trump’s 2025 presidential inauguration. Military musicians from the US Marine Corps and the US Army will also perform during the formal dinner. They will include “The President’s Own” United States Marine Band and “The Commandant’s Own” United States Marine Drum and Bugle Corps. The United States Army Chorus and the United States Army Strings are also on the programme. Red will dominate the East Room. The First Lady’s office said the décor draws on the colour’s longstanding cultural significance in China. Urns will hold red blossoms, while tables will be covered in rich red linens and decorated with dahlias and ranunculus. The tables will also feature vermeil from the White House collection and pieces from the Reagan State Service. The arrangement is intended to place Chinese cultural references alongside White House traditions, from the flowers and table settings to the formal dinner service. The wine toast points back to Nixon’s 1972 visit to Beijing, when he and Zhou raised a toast that the White House release calls the “Toast to Peace”. The release says the same American sparkling wine served at that gathering is still enjoyed at White House functions. Nixon’s visit was a major step in the opening of relations between Washington and Beijing. Thursday’s dinner uses that history as a reference point for welcoming Xi and Peng, even as the evening’s menu, music and setting mark the occasion as a White House state dinner.

articles.title: From Fibre to Future: Weaving Sustainability into India's Textile Growth
articles.description: Giriraj SinghAs India targets a US$350 billion textile and apparel industry by 2030, sustainability is moving from the margins to the centre of its competitiveness strategy. For a sector spanning fibre, yarn, fabric, processing, apparel, technical textiles and made-ups, sustainability is increasingly becoming a question of competitiveness, market access and responsible growth.When Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that “The World is adopting the vision of Fashion for Environment and Empowerment, and India can lead the way in this regard,” he pointed to a transformation increasingly visible across India’s textile landscape.The textile sector is a major employment engine, directly supporting over 49 million livelihoods. Its domestic market is valued at about US$196 billion and is projected to reach US$250 billion by 2030, while India is targeting US$100 billion in textile exports by the same year.The Ministry of Textiles’ sustainability agenda reflects this dual reality. It is built around a simple proposition: India should not have to choose between growth and sustainability. Instead, cleaner production, resource efficiency, circularity and responsible manufacturing are set to become the foundation of the textile sector’s next growth chapter.Why sustainability has become a competitiveness issueGlobal brands are setting increasingly ambitious sustainability targets for their supply chains. Consumers are showing greater interest in reused, repaired and recycled products, while policymakers in major export markets are introducing requirements around environmental performance, recycled content, traceability, chemicals, water and energy use. India’s climate commitments—including 500GW of non-fossil energy capacity, 50% of energy requirements from renewables and net zero emissions by 2070—are also steering the textile sector towards a low-carbon growth trajectory. For Indian exporters, sustainability is therefore moving beyond a peripheral compliance issue and becoming an integral part of industrial competitiveness.India also starts from a position of strength, with a large manufacturing base, diverse raw materials, technical capabilities, an established recycling and reuse ecosystem, a growing start-up landscape and a wide network of clusters, research institutions and industry associations. Circularity is not entirely new to India. Traditions such as rafugari, kantha, godhadis, chindi durries and khesh weaving have embedded repair, reuse and repurposing in communities for generations.India’s hosting of the World Circular Economy Forum 2026 further reflects this larger shift, bringing governments, industry, innovators and experts together to turn ideas into partnerships and scalable solutions.Turning textile waste into a circular opportunityOne of the clearest areas to put circularity into practice is textile waste. A Ministry study from 2026, covering 15 states and more than 250 stakeholder interactions, estimated annual textile waste generation at 70.73 lakh tonnes. More than 70 per cent is already recovered and routed into recycling, downcycling or upcycling streams, with recovery of pre-consumer waste exceeding 95 per cent.The larger gap is post-consumer waste, where collection, segregation and economically viable recovery systems remain less developed. The study estimated that India’s textile recycling market could reach about US$3.5 billion by 2030, with opportunities across collection, sorting, fibre recovery, recycling, upcycling, repair and sustainable manufacturing, with the potential to generate around one lakh green jobs.The Ministry is moving beyond quantifying the problem to building the infrastructure and market mechanisms needed to close the loop. Textile Recovery Facilities are being piloted in multiple cities, while textile-waste mapping is identifying the need for stronger collection and sorting systems and policy solutions for blended and non-recyclable materials. A textile-waste management pilot in Navi Mumbai, implemented by the Textiles Committee in partnership with Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation, Saahas Foundation and women’s self-help groups, diverted more than 3,323 kg of textile waste monthly from landfill and incineration, reached over 12,000 families and installed more than 80 collection bins. It also produced over 1,000 sample and upcycled products. Through a partnership between the Textiles Committee, Government e-Marketplace (GeM) and SCOPE, certified upcycled textile products are being brought into public procurement. Thirty-one upcyclers have been certified under the Upcycled Textile Mark, with 27 categories and 40 products live on GeM, helping create an assured market for circular products.Cleaner production: water, energy and chemicalsCircularity is only one part of the sustainability story. Much of the environmental footprint of textiles is created during manufacturing and processing, making water, energy and chemicals equally important. The agenda of eliminating hazardous chemicals is being taken up through a major programme with UNIDO, the Global Environment Facility and other partners. The project aims to reduce hazardous chemicals while improving energy, water and greenhouse-gas performance. Its targets include reducing 10,530 tonnes of toxic chemicals directly and 21,000 tonnes indirectly, while mitigating 147,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent directly and 294,000 tonnes indirectly. It is also designed to directly reach 40,000 people, 60 per cent of whom are expected to be women. At the infrastructure level, sustainability is being built into the sector’s future industrial geography. Seven PM MITRA Parks, with an expected investment of about US$10 billion, are envisaged with integrated water, wastewater and common processing infrastructure.From pilots to scale: policy, technology and MSMEsFor sustainability to become mainstream, pilots must move into factories and clusters. This is particularly important because a large part of the textile ecosystem comprises MSMEs, which may face constraints in accessing technology, finance, data and technical expertise. The Ministry constituted an ESG Task Force in July 2023, bringing together government bodies, industry associations, chambers, multilateral agencies, innovators, brands and academia. Its work focuses on harmonised certification, cluster handholding, awareness and capacity building, sustainable fashion technology, and the use of artificial intelligence and digitalisation for data and traceability. The ESG Task Force has supported the EU-India Resource Efficiency & Circular Economy Initiative (EU-I RECEI), implemented through GIZ, covering a national assessment of textile waste, a circular economy roadmap for Tamil Nadu, an MSME toolkit for Panipat and a standard operating procedure for Textile Recovery Facilities. A separate UNEP-led programme is providing life-cycle assessment and eco-innovation training and technical assistance to SMEs in the Surat and Karur clusters.Technology and innovation are also long-term enablers. The National Technical Textiles Mission supports research into waste-to-fibre technologies and conversion of textile waste and bio-residues into advanced green materials. At IIT Delhi’s Panipat campus, the Atal Centre of Textile Recycling and Sustainability is undertaking research and technology transfer, including recycling heat-resistant aramid fibre waste used in defence and aerospace applications. At Bharat Tex 2026, sustainability-focused research on traceable hemp fibre, circular business models and wheat straw as a forest-free alternative for man-made cellulosic fibres further highlighted the breadth of innovation emerging around the sector.Tex-Eco: sustainability within the growth architectureThe Union Budget 2026–27 provided a strong policy signal. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced an Integrated Programme for the labour-intensive textile sector, with Tex-Eco placing sustainability alongside fibre security, manufacturing expansion, traditional clusters, handlooms, handicrafts and skilling—not as a separate environmental programme, but as part of the sector’s growth architecture. The proposed Tex-Eco Initiative brings together four strategic pillars: resource recovery and recycling infrastructure; water stewardship and decarbonisation; institutionalising sustainability and building capability; and innovation, digital enablement and knowledge systems. Textile Recycling Mega-Hubs and Textile Recovery Facilities would support collection, sorting, grading and routing of textile waste. Water and decarbonisation measures would support ZLD, renewable energy, low-emission boilers and resource-efficient technologies. An India Sustainability Mark is proposed to strengthen market credibility, alongside assurance, compliance, capacity building and demand generation.Building an ESG ecosystemBehind these interventions is a broader institutional shift. A dedicated Sustainability Section within the Ministry of Textiles acts as a focal point for sustainable and circular practices, resource efficiency, environmental impact reduction, green technologies and responsible production. The government is positioned not only as regulator, but also as facilitator, leader and implementing partner. The ESG agenda also goes beyond the environmental dimension. Worker welfare, formalisation, green jobs and a just transition sit alongside decarbonisation, water stewardship, chemical safety and circularity, while governance priorities include standards, traceability, disclosure, certification and assurance.The next chapterIndia’s textile sustainability journey is entering a critical phase, with the focus now on stronger post-consumer collection, recycling infrastructure, resource-efficient manufacturing, commercialisation of green technologies, credible measurement and traceability, and stronger markets for recycled and upcycled products. A proposed Sustainability Alliance would bring together government, UN agencies, financial institutions, industry, MSMEs and academia around these priorities.The direction is increasingly clear: sustainability must work for a factory owner as much as for the environment, for an exporter as much as the consumer, and for a large integrated park as much as for a small enterprise. This can improve resource productivity, unlock access to demanding global markets, spur new businesses around recycling and green technologies, and generate employment.For a nation on track to nearly double its textile and apparel market by 2030, sustainability is not about slowing growth. It is about powering the next wave of growth—cleaner, more circular, more resilient and ultimately more competitive.The author is the Union Minister of Textiles. The views expressed are personal.

articles.title: Current Affairs One- Liner: 23rd September 2026
articles.description: National: On 17 Septemb er 2026, the Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana completed 11 years of implementation. Launched on 17 September 2015, the scheme uses District Mineral Foundation funds to improve the lives of people affected by mining. More tha n 4.70 lakh projects worth over ₹1 lakh crore have been sanctioned in areas such as drinking water, healthcare, education, sanitation, livelihoods and environmental conservation. The Ministry of Mines oversees the scheme, while district authorities implement projects according to local requirements. On 20 September 2026, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports organised the nationwide Rashtriya Sankalp Samaroh under the 100 Weeks Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Abhiyan. Implemented through MY Bharat and partner organisations at more than 1,000 locations, the programme involved pledge-taking, signature campaigns and youth discussions. Its objective is to prevent substance abuse, promote healthy lifestyles and encourage young people to lead community awareness activities. The campaign includes themes such as My Health, My Pride, Fit Youth, Addiction-Free Youth and Life Skills Month. On 22 September 2026, Union Jal Shakti Minister C. R. Patil launched Swachh Seva Aankalan to assess sanitation standards and public participation in rur al areas. The initiative evaluates cleanliness, solid and liquid waste management, plastic-waste control and maintenance of community sanitation facilities. It supports Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen Phase II, particularly the sustainability of ODF Plus villages. The assessment will encourage healthy competition among villages and recognise gram panchayats demonstrating effective sanitation governance, sustainable waste-management practices and active community participation. On 16 September 2026, Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh virtually inaugurated India’s 51st Doppler Weather Radar at Jamadarpali in Sambalp ur, Odisha. Developed under Mission Mausam, the Make in India radar covers approximately 250 kilometres and provides updated observations every ten minutes. It will strengthen forecasts of thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, cyclones and other extreme weather events across western Odisha and neighbouring regions. Odisha now has three Doppler Weather Radars, located at Gopalpur, Paradip and Sambalpur. O n 22 September 2026, Assam highlighted that it supports nearly 80% of India’s greater one-horned rhinoceros population. The animals are conc entrated mainly in Kaziranga National Park, Orang National Park, Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary and Manas National Park. Anti-poaching measures, habitat restoration and scientific population monitoring have contributed to improved conservation. The greater one-horned rhinoceros is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, and is classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. On 22 September 2026, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare reaffirmed India’s commitment to eliminating hepatitis B and C as public-health threats by 2030. The strategy focuses on hepatitis B vaccination, screening of high-risk groups, safe blood transfusion, infection-control measures and access to antiviral treatment. These activities are implemented through the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme. India is also expanding testing among pregnant women, healthcare workers and vulnerable communities to prevent transmission, liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. On 22 September 2026, the Union government announced plans to replace Shastri Bhawan and Krishi Bhawan in New Delhi with modern Karta vya Bhawan complexes under the Central Vista redevelopment programme. The new buildings will consolidate Union ministries and provide modern security, energy-efficiency and digital facilities. The project is expected to improve coordination between departments, reduce expenditure on rented premises and address infrastructure limitations in the existing buildings. Ministries currently functioning from the two buildi ngs will be temporarily relocated before redevelopment begins. On 23 September 2026, Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana completed eight years. Launched on 23 September 2018, PM-JAY provides eligible families with cashless hospitalisation cover of up to ₹5 lakh per family annually for secondary and tertiary healthcare. The National Health Authority implements the programme with state health agencies. Treatment is provided through empanelled public and private hospitals. The scheme seeks to reduce catastrophic healthcare expenditure and has also been expanded to eligible senior citizens aged 70 years and above. On 22 Sept ember 2026, the Ministry of Education released the NIRF 2026 Sustainable Development Goals ranking to assess the contribu tion of higher-education institutions to social and environmental sustainability. The framework evaluates clean energy, water conservation, waste management, climate action, gender equality, inclusive education and community engagement. Introduced as a specialised category under the National Institutional Ranking Framework, it encourages universities and colleges to incorporate sustainability into teaching, research, campus administration, infrastructure development and institutional governance. On 22 September 2026, the Assam government announced that all state-government offices would operate through the e-Office system from 1 January 20 27. The initiative will replace physical files with electronic records, digital approvals and online movement of documents. Its objectives are to improve administrative efficiency, increase transparency, reduce delays and lower expenditure on paper and physical storage. Government departments have been directed to digitise existing records and train employees before the deadline as part of Assam’s wider digital-governance programme. On 22 Septe mber 2026, Andhra Pradesh Police launched an artificial intelligence-enabled drone portal and the SafeStay mobile application. The drone port al will help authorities register, monitor and regulate drone operations while identifying unauthorised activities in sensitive areas. SafeStay is intended to improve the verification and security of guests staying in hotels, lodges and other accommodation establishments. The initiatives aim to strengthen surveillance, support crime prevention, improve emergency response and allow police agencies to process an d analyse information more efficiently. On 23 September 2026, the Delhi government launched the DURGA scheme to introduce approximately 1,300 pink electric autorickshaws for wo men drivers. The programme seeks to improve women’s participation in public transport while providing safer last-mile connectivity to female passengers. Eligible women will receive support for obtaining and operating electric autorickshaws, including access to designated permits and financial assistance. The initiative also supports Delhi’s electric-vehicle policy by reducing vehicular emissions and encouraging the transition towards cleaner urban transportation. On 22 Septe mber 2026, Jagruti Rehabilitation Centre received the National Clinical Excellence Award for its contribution to mental-health treatmen t, addiction recovery and rehabilitation. The award recognised its patient-centred treatment programmes, multidisciplinary care and efforts to improve access to behavioural-health services. The institution provides psychiatric consultation, counselling, rehabilitation and de-addiction support through trained healthcare professionals. The recognition highlights the importance of quality standards, ethical treatment, professional supervision and evidence-based clinical practices in India’s mental-health and substance-abuse rehabilitation sector. International: In September 202 6, UN Women and the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs released The Gender Snapshot 2026. The repo rt found that one in three national institutions responsible for gender equality had lost institutional authority during the previous two years, while one in four experienced budget reductions. It warned that no indicator under Sustainable Development Goal 5 was on track for achievement by 2030. The report recommended stronger institutions, adequate financing and greater participation of women in political and economic decision-making. On 18 September 2026, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement to strengthen defence cooperation in the Arctic and North Atlantic regions. It permits the United States to modernise and expand activities at Pituffik Space Base and establish additional defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. Greenland will remain under Danish sovereignty, and the agreement has no fixed expiry date. It also prevents non-NATO countries from establishing permanent military installations in Greenland, reflecting the region’s growing strategic importance. On 22 September 2026, a World Economic Forum survey placed India at the top of the global growth outlook among major economies. Respondents highlighted strong domestic demand, expanding digital infrastructure, public capital expenditure and continued growth in manufacturing and services. The findings indicated greater confidence in India’s medium-term economic prospects than in several economies facing weak demand or geopolitical uncertainty. However, the survey also identified employment creation, inflation, global trade disruptions and private-sector investment as challenges affecting the sustainability of India’s growth. On 22 September 2026 , Bangladesh appointed senior diplomat Asad Alam Siam as its new High Commissioner to India. The appointment was made by the G overnment of Bangladesh as part of its diplomatic postings. As High Commissioner, he will manage political, economic, trade and security relations with India. His responsibilities will include cooperation in connectivity, border management, water sharing, energy and people-to-people relations. The posting is significant because India and Bangladesh share extensive geographical, economic, cultural and strategic ties. Banking: On 22 September 2 026, the government introduced a CGTMSE-backed guarantee mechanism for financing conducted through Trade Receivables Discounting System platforms. The measure will reduce the risk faced by banks and other financiers when discounting invoices raised by micro and small enterprises. TReDS allows MSMEs to obtain working capital by selling approved invoices to financiers before their due dates. The guarantee cover is expected to increase financier participation, improve liquidity for small businesses and reduce their dependence on collateral-based borrowing and delayed payments from large buyers. Economy: In September 2026, the Competition Commission of India approved the acquisition of Rajasthan Royals, Paarl Royals and Barbados Royals by Westview Cricke t Limited and Poonawalla Sports and Fitness Private Limited. The franchises participate in professional T20 leagues in India, South Africa and the Caribbean. Westview Cricket is registered in the United Kingdom, while Poonawalla Sports is owned by Adar Poonawalla. The approval followed an examination of whether the proposed ownership change could adversely affect competition in the relevant sports and commercial markets. On 22 September 2026, Fitch Ratings raised India’s GDP growth forecast for FY2026-27 from 6.4% to 6.9%. The revision followed stronger-than-expected economic growth supported by domestic consumption, investment and resilient industrial activity. Fitch referred to India’s 7.8% growth during the June quarter while assessing inflation and monetary-policy conditions. The agency also expected the Reserve Bank of India to consider policy tightening if inflationary pressures increased. The revised forecast reinforced India’s position among the fastest-growing major economies. On 22 September 2 026, S&P Global raised India’s GDP growth forecast for FY2026-27 from 6.6% to 7%. The agency cited strong household consumption, industrial activity, infrastructure expenditure and favourable domestic demand. The revised estimate reflected confidence in India’s economic resilience despite global trade uncertainty and geopolitical risks. However, S&P noted that inflation, international energy prices, employment conditions and external demand remained important variables. For examination purposes, S&P projected 7% growth, while Fitch projected 6.9% growth for FY27. Sports: On 23 September 20 26, India secured its first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis at the 2026 Asian Games. The achievement marked India’s entry o nto the continental podium in a sport traditionally dominated by East Asian countries. Soft tennis uses a soft rubber ball and includes singles, doubles and team competitions. The medal expanded India’s achievements beyond its traditional Asian Games strengths. It is expected to encourage greater investment, specialised coaching and participation in soft tennis at the national and grassroots levels. On 23 Septe mber 2026, Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu won the silver medal in the women’s 49 kg category at the Asian Games 2026. Her final position was determined by the combined total of her best successful lifts in the snatch and clean-and-jerk events. The Olympic medallist’s performance added an important medal to India’s Asian Games tally and reaffirmed her position among Asia’s leading weightlifters. The competition featured top athletes from participating Asian countries in the 49 kg weight category. On 23 Septembe r 2026, the fourth day of the Asian Games produced medals for India across events including weightlifting, shooting and soft tennis. Mirab ai Chanu’s silver medal in the women’s 49 kg weightlifting category was among the major achievements, while India also secured its first-ever Asian Games medal in soft tennis. The day’s performances added to India’s overall medal tally and demonstrated the country’s competitive strength across established and emerging sports. The results were officially incorporated into the Asian Games medal table. Military Exercise: On 21 September 2 026, the 18th edition of the India-Mongolia joint military exercise Nomadic Elephant began at Pithoragarh in Uttarakhand. It in volves contingents from the Indian Army and the Mongolian Armed Forces. The exercise focuses on joint tactical operations, counterterrorism, peacekeeping and interoperability in mountainous terrain under a United Nations mandate. Training activities include field exercises, combat drills, casualty evacuation and coordination between participating forces. India and Mongolia organise the exercise alternately to strengthen defence cooperation and exchange operational experience. In September 202 6, the Indian Army deployed its AH-64E Apache attack helicopters during Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, the annual joint military exercise bet ween India and the United States. The helicopters supported air-land integration, reconnaissance, close-air support and coordinated battlefield operations. The exercise brings together personnel from the Indian Army and the US Army to improve interoperability in conventional and counterterrorism operations. The Apache fleet’s participation demonstrated India’s growing ability to integrate advanced army-aviation assets with ground forces during joint operations. Science and Technology: On 22 September 2026, the India Meteorological Department reported that a depression over the Bay of Bengal was moving towards the Andhra Pradesh-Odisha co ast and could intensify into a deep depression. The system was expected to produce heavy rainfall, strong winds and rough sea conditions. Fishermen were advised not to enter affected waters, while disaster-response teams were placed on alert. Early warnings were issued to coastal districts to facilitate evacuations and minimise damage to crops, houses, fishing boats and essential infrastructure. On 22 September 202 6, birdwatchers reported a leucistic great cormorant at Ameenpur Lake in Telangana. Leucism is a genetic condition that causes parti al or complete loss of pigmentation in feathers while generally retaining normal eye colour, unlike albinism. The unusual sighting is valuable for documenting genetic variations among birds and the biodiversity of the lake. Ameenpur Lake is recognised as a Biodiversity Heritage Site and supports numerous resident and migra tory bird species, highlighting the importance of protecting urban wetlands. On 22 September 2026, Hurricane Polo intensified into a Category 5 storm over the eastern Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Mexico. Category 5 is the highest classi fication on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale and indicates sustained winds of at least 252 kilometres per hour. Mexican authorities issued marine and coastal warnings because of dangerous waves, strong winds and heavy rainfall. Meteorological agencies monitored the hurricane’s projected route, while disaster-management authorities prepared evacuation and emergency-response measures for potentially affected coastal communities. Defence: On 21 Septembe r 2026, the Ministry of Defence signed a ₹586-crore contract with Accurate Industrial Controls Private Limited for Auxiliary Power Units fo r the Indian Army’s T-72 and T-90 tanks. The agreement was signed in New Delhi in the presence of Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh. APUs allow tank communications, electronics and other systems to operate without running the main engine, reducing fuel consumption, noise and thermal signatures. The procurement promotes indigenous defence manufacturing and improves the operational endurance of India’s armoured formations.
